lines: It names no group and no measurement, and a single person has one answer.
``How many hours did Granite Falls students sleep last night?''
A statistic --- it describes the 80-member sample, not all 1,600 members.
Time or cost --- reaching every one of 1,600 members would take far too long.
Method 1. Response bias --- the leading wording pushes people toward yes, so it
overestimates: 74\% against 45\%, or 1,110 card holders against 675.
Reversed arrow: good grades are what let a student stay on a team, so grades put
students into the sport group --- that pushes the athletes' percent up on its own.
Leading --- ``Don't you agree'' pushes toward yes, so the wording is not neutral.
Double-barrelled --- it asks about books and picnic tables in one item.
A is observational, B is an experiment: who decided the groups --- families chose in A,
a generator assigned in B. Observing is how B collected data, not how it built groups.
Study B. Random assignment made the groups alike at the start, so the program is the
only difference left. Study A's bigger gap earns only ``is associated with.''
Families who chose to sign up were already readers, so A's program group started
ahead. Self-selection inflates the gap; in B nobody chose, so that head start is gone.
Nonresponse bias --- the 75\% who never returned it cared less about a dog park.
It overestimates by 30 percentage points, or $504 - 288 = 216$ households.
Twice the responses, the same wrong 70\%: a larger sample does not remove bias.
Draw a random sample of households and follow up by phone or in person until nearly
all of them answer. That removes the nonresponse bias, which size never did.
Stratified. A full numbered list exists and the grades are expected to differ, so
drawing at random within each grade guarantees all three are represented in proportion.
Survey. The question has a fixed yes/no answer and needs many students, so a short
written instrument given to the whole sample can be counted quickly.
Chance never chose her advisory --- the other 810 students could not be asked --- so the
match is luck: the same room could have missed by 20 points and nothing would warn her.
She may say only that 40\% of her own advisory wants a garden club.
